utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you. Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Everyone is here except Stephane Bourgon. If there are at any time problems with interpretation, please draw our attention straight away, all right? We can bring in the witness, I suppose. Are there any preliminaries? I mean -- we will be handing down later on our decision on protective measures and safe conduct for Witness PW-115. I think I anticipated yesterday what the outcome is going to be. Both requests are being granted, both safe custody and the protective measures asked for, all right?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Have you had a good rest?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I really didn't sleep so well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's not good news, but we are going to make a big effort today, all of us, to try and bring your testimony to an end as quickly as possible. You will recall that yesterday Mr. Krgovic, who is lead counsel defending General Gvero here, was still cross-examining you when we had to adjourn. He will very soon now continue with his cross-examination and bring it to an end. He will then be followed by Madam Fauveau for General Miletic and the Defence team for General Pandurevic, although not necessarily in that order. Yes. Mr. Krgovic, good morning to you. You may proceed with your cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honour. I just wanted to ask the usher to move the screen a little bit so that I can see the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That I think we can do. However, then I want to make sure in the public gallery that you do not allow anyone to sit in a position where they could get a transversal of you off the witness. I see you nodding, so I know that you are understanding exactly what I mean. We are taking all the necessary precautions - you can put your mind at rest - to protect you and your identity, Witness. Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, do you remember that yesterday I asked you about that first day, the 6th of July, and I'm sure you remember what you answered. I'm going to continue with the chronology, and I will put questions to you similar to those of the Prosecutor. Specifically, I'm going to ask you about the events from the 6th onwards until the 9th or the 10th of July. My line of questions will be related to your previous statements. So I would just like to ask you to confirm if I have interpreted properly what you said earlier. Could you please tell me, after the 6th of July you heard that forces of the army of Republika Srpska had advanced and you had withdrawn to Viogor; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We actually went towards the village of Suceska, Viogor. There's a large number of villages there in a small area. And after we saw UNPROFOR who had began to withdraw towards Srebrenica, we went after them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After that you heard that soldiers of the army, of the B and H, carried out a counter-attack and briefly managed to recapture starting positions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I would like to show Exhibit 4D00048. [Interpretation] This is page 2 of this statement. Could we show the witness the B/C/S version, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, it's a sentence somewhere in the middle. It starts with: "In the meantime, we heard that Chetniks had advanced and moved towards Srebrenica and the Slapovici settlement," and then we skip and bit and then it says: "That's where we heard that members of our army returned the Chetniks to their starting positions, and soon after, our forces returned to the starting positions." Do you see where that is written?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes. I couldn't recall that right away but, yes, that is correct. These were the positions -- I actually knew where the UNPROFOR soldiers were. That's probably where they were.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: After that you heard from soldiers, from your soldiers, that NATO aeroplanes would bomb the Serbian army and tanks and that your soldiers were planning, if this were to happen, to carry out a counter-action to retake lost positions. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time since I saw the statement. Can I please look at it again?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Yes. It's a sentence starting from "in the morning," it's lower down, "we heard from the soldiers that NATO aeroplanes were expected to bomb."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There was a large crowd of people, so we probably heard it from the soldiers. That's the answer. And probably also from UNPROFOR.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: This statement in your -- what you said in your previous statement, then, is correct.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. After that, you went towards the direction of the village of Susnjari where you found your father.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We went with my father -- well, my mother, my sister, the other refugees. From the camp we were going in the direction of Suceska. These were people from other villages too. I don't know how I lost my father. I don't know whether he went to carry something or it take something. I'm not sure. Clothing, something like that. But we got lost, and my mother and my sister went to Potocari, and I went with my uncle and another cousin towards the village of Susnjari where I met my father. I think that he had gone to some other cousin's or relative's house to take something from there, clothing or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Then you found your father at Susnjari when they were lining up in their brigade. He belonged to the 284th Brigade of the B and H army; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think yesterday that I responded to this question, and I will give you the answer again. I don't remember the exact number. Maybe I recalled it at the time, but now it's been 10 years ago. But I think that brigade or that unit, I don't know what it was, was at Cerska or Konjevic Polje. When he came to Srebrenica, I think that he -- I don't know whether they were demobilised. I don't know the correct term for it, but they were inactive. I know that my father wasn't summoned anywhere. He was with us the entire time. When we got there, he probably knew the people who were lining up, those people who had been in his unit. So I tried to join him in those ranks.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... 00046. 4D. [Interpretation] Your Honours, is this being broadcast publicly? Because there is the name of the witness at the top of this piece of paper. Perhaps we need to go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I am told by our registrar that it is not. All right. Of course, if you make reference to anything contained in it that would still expose his identity, then obviously we're going to have to rethink the whole matter. And thank you for raising the issue, Mr. Krgovic. It shows that you all share the concerns that the Trial Chamber has.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you please look at this part of your statement. It's somewhere in the middle. It begins with the words "after that."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'll trying to see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: It's at the bottom of the page. It says: "After that, we moved towards the direction of the village of Susnjari where in a line-up I found my father, and he was in the 284th Brigade."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot find it. Just give me a moment, please. Maybe someone can show me where it is. You cannot see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can we please scroll up, because you cannot see it. Now we see it. Witness, what line is it from the bottom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you. Just one moment. It's the 9th line from the bottom.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: On that occasion I hid.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, no, after that. "Afterwards we moved on towards the village of Susnjari where in a line-up of his brigade I found my father, and he was in the 284th Brigade."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: And that was that?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do remember that. I don't recall this particular number, but I probably recalled it correctly then. I knew what the number was. I don't know the number of the brigade now, but then I probably could remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, then when you were in Susnjari, that night all members of the army were lined up, especially men who were above the -- who were born after 1980. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an assumption. Perhaps that's how it was, but there were a lot of women as well, younger -- young children also.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Exhibit 4D00048.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'm wondering the relevance of the make-up of the column. It's not really something that's disputed, and we've gone over this before, but ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I mean, I do have an idea, but, Mr. Krgovic, perhaps you could explain it better. What's -- in other words, it's being put to you that this is not a matter that has been actively contested by the Prosecution; rather, indirectly they are acknowledging it as a fact so why are you pursuing it? This is basically what -- what is being -- If I read you well, Mr. McCloskey, because if I'm not reading you well, then please correct me.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Absolutely. It's in the indictment how many people we thought were armed, the make-up of the column, you know, the -- all these issues as -- of course anything going to the witness's credibility, but I don't see that quite.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Krgovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if the Prosecution accepts that this was a military column, we will drop up the line of questioning regarding that topic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey. I find it difficult to anticipate your answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Well, I can tell you, yes, it was a military column. You don't see any war crimes being charged on the attack of this column. And the head of this column was a military column and it did a hell of an attack on 16 July and many Serb soldiers were killed. That's been part of the case from the beginning. It's in the indictment. It's in Mr. Butler's report. It's been fundamental to -- even what the witnesses are saying, like this witness. So --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but the witness was in the back of the column.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: But that's not -- we've been very clear on that. That's -- that's part of our case. So I don't have any problem agreeing to any of that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Anyway, Mr. Krgovic, I suggest that you bring this area of questioning -- of questions to a very quick end and move to something where the Prosecution and yourselves are in confrontation.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if I may seek another clarification, and that will be my last question, is the Prosecution contesting the fact that everybody in the column who was born after the year 1980 was mobilised and that a general mobilisation preceded that event in Srebrenica and that everybody born after the year 1980 was mobilised? And this is what I want to hear from this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Completely -- this is something completely different than what you were asking the witness about. But do you want to comment on that, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yeah, we're talking mobilisation and those issues. You know, I wouldn't mind talking outside the presence of the witness if it will help narrow the issues of this case, because even that issue is something I don't really have much dispute with.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Anyway, then if this is the area which -- in which you are interested, could you please address this particular area and forget about the other one. And it seems that the witness is very anxious to answer your question as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, let's me ask you --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Can I say something before you put any questions to me?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Let me put the question first and then I'll give you an opportunity to say whatever you want. Can you please look at the paragraph starting with the words, and this is somewhere towards the end, and the beginning of the sentence is "under Susnjari."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: "On that night, all members of the army and able-bodied men who were born after the year 1980 were lined up under Susnjari." Can you see that this is what it reads?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sure that they must have been able-bodied as soon as they set out to walk through the forest. They could not have been disabled.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: What do you mean by "able-bodied"?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Militarily able-bodied.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: So you're asking about militarily able-bodied. It says "members of the army and able-bodied." It doesn't say militarily able-bodied.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: Is it correct what it says here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm reading the sentence back to you. I'm not a linguist, but I understand the sentence, I can interpret it, and I'm reading it back to you. The sentence begins with "at Susnjari," then the next word is illegible, and then it says "members of the army and able-bodied men." It doesn't say fit for the army. It just says fit, fit to -- to walk through the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But it says those who were born after the year 1980.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nobody ever checked when they were born. If they volunteered, they were lined up, but there were also women and children. But if you're implying that all of these people were troops, were members of the army, then you are walking on very thin ground. When I mentioned the line-up, I mentioned this not as a military expert because I'm not a military expert. This was done in order to form the column in order to be able to go through the minefields and avoid mines. I did not see any cattle being let about before the column to activate the mines, but I heard that this had happened. So the line-up was done in order to put the column in order, and that was the only intention.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: So this is correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is correct, and I am adding something else to that sentence, to that part of the statement. It is correct and I am adding some more detail to it. The line-up of the army was carried out. There were a lot of people. It was getting dark. I couldn't see everything. I was in that part of the column, and I'm sure that there were a lot of men who were born after the year 1980, but there are also younger children.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: But you were not a member of the same unit as your father.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me explain. There were a lot of people there. Let me explain. Although I don't know whether you care about my explanation. When the shelling started --

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm not interested in the line-up.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Still, I want to tell you about it. I am not avoiding giving you an answer. I'm not protecting anybody. I'm not justifying anybody for anything. I just want to give my answer. There were a lot of people. The shelling started. There was chaos. People wanted to enter the forest as soon as possible in order to protect themselves from -- from shelling, and in that chaos I lost my father. I stayed behind with the civilians. And then I caught up with my father later on. The army wouldn't let people go through. They wouldn't let the civilians go through. They told the civilians to stay behind. But people will be people. They wanted to get hold of some soldier because they thought that they would be better protected. We felt that -- that we were a burden upon them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: I'm talking about the line-up in Susnjari, and I'm asking whether you were together with your father in the same unit. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honours. I don't have any more questions for this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Krgovic. Mr. Haynes, who is lead counsel appearing for General Pandurevic will now be questioning you, cross-examining you. Mr. Haynes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Good morning. I only have to ask you questions about one very small issue, and it's about the trucks in which you were transported. I take it from the evidence that you've given that you were transported in the same trucks from Sandici to Bratunac as you were from Bratunac to Petkovci and then from Petkovci away from the school.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me tell you and let me explain what happened. The group of trucks, some five or six of them, we got on the lorries and I can tell you about my lorry, that I didn't leave the lorry in Bratunac. All of us who were captured and who were on that truck were taken back to the place where we were captured, where we had surrendered and then onto the school. When we entered the school -- actually, we got on a lorry, and I don't know what kind of a lorry it was. It was dark, and I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: But both lorries that you got on had a tarpaulin cover and were able to house about a hundred people in your estimation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The first set of lorries that took us to Bratunac and those that took us back to the school, those were big lorries that could hold anything between a hundred and 200 people. And for the second one, I don't know how big it was. It was fully loaded, but I don't know how many people there were on that second lorry.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. When you were able to see the lorries, you could tell that they were 20-tonne trailer trucks, couldn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That was clear. Those were the largest possible lorries. They didn't have separate trailers. I thought that they would be 20-tonne trucks, approximately. That was my estimate.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And you could tell that the tarpaulin covers were yellow in colour and that on the outside of the lorry was written the phrase "Tuzla Transport."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember that, but I don't know whether this featured on all the lorries. This I saw on the lorries when we got on them from the meadow, but when we were taken for execution, these lorries were covered with tarpaulins. I don't know what colour they were and whether there were any inscriptions on them. I can't remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: Of course. Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So it's Madam Fauveau who is last to go.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone for the Presiding Judge, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau will be the last counsel to cross-examine you. Madam Fauveau is appearing for General Miletic. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, yesterday you mentioned the school in Petkovci, and you said that back at the time when you were detained in the school you didn't know it was the Petkovci school. Is it fair to say, indeed, that you learned that it was the Petkovci school when you arrived in the ABiH-controlled territory?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I believe that I answered that yesterday. I learned subsequently. I don't know when. Either from the people in the school who hailed from the area or maybe later on in the village. In any case, I learnt subsequently, but I can't recall all the details. In any case, when we first arrived I never even knew that this was a school, let alone what its name was.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you testified in the Milosevic case. I'm going to read out to you what you said in the Milosevic case regarding the time when you learned that that was the Petkovci school. Transcript page 3675, 17th of December. This is what you testified: [In English] "After we escaped, when we reached the free territory people were saying that we were as we were going through these villages. They were saying it could be this or it could be that, but then when we entered this place we knew it was a school. So I remember that we were talking to people and they said it could be Petkovci. And afterwards I went there with the investigators, so I confirmed that was it."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Maybe that was my recollection at the time. This may have been what I said, but what is important is the fact that this was a school and that later on I could confirm that fact. However, I don't know what the relevance of the name of the school is. You can ask me anything, but I can't see the relevance of the school's name.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown P1729.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Yesterday, transcript page 45, you recognise or identified this building as being the school where you were detained; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's the school where we were detained, but you can see only one of its parts and part of the entrance.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Isn't it fair to say that you were not able to really see the building very well, the building where you were detained when you arrived on the location in July 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't understand your question. What did I not see?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that you were not able to see the building very well from outside, I mean the building where you were detained, when you arrived there in 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I saw the building, but I didn't really care what it looked like at the moment when we were being beaten and ill-treated. I really didn't care about the appearance of the building.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 4D53. This is the statement given to the OTP in August 1995.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One question. Let's go into private session for a very short while.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You mentioned, or you stated that -- you put it to the witness that he testified in Milosevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... under a pseudonym in Milosevic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Mr. President. He testified as Witness 1401, B-1401, but indeed it might be better to remain in private session because his name is mentioned in the statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was only concerned in the sense that he could be then identified in a direct manner.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, I don't think so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is not the case. So you prefer to stay in private session for this line of questions now?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just for the statement. There's only the initials, but still.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 4D53. Can we turn to page 6. It was also the page 6 in the B/C/S version. The penultimate paragraph.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you testified on the 12th and the 13th of August, 1995. That is one month after the events. Or you stated, rather. [In English] "I saw one building in front of me. I do not remember exactly what it looked like. I was so close to the building that I could not see if anything else was around the building. It was getting dark out by this time." [Interpretation] Is it therefore fair to say that you were not able to see what the building looked like?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're trying to say that I have no clue, but I will tell you. I mean, I will explain. The stairs that we went down, that's where the people were beaten up. I remember that perfectly well. The entrance, I remember the stairs in the building, which direction they go into. I remember the classroom I was in. It was a classroom for pupils. And I said all of that in my statement, and after that I went and reconfirmed that. Perhaps I do not remember -- or did not remember the facade or what was outside, but I perfectly remember all of it. I think that what you are trying to ask me to absolutely irrelevant, really. I mean, I'm really speaking very sincerely.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: My question concerned the outside. From outside were you able to recognise the building, because you said that you identified the building in the photograph, and that is taken from outside.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not just one photograph. There are plenty of photographs, both from the outside and from the inside. So I was able to identify it like that.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Once again Exhibit P1729. Now, when you look at this photograph from the outside, just this photograph, can you say with accuracy that this is the school in which you were detained?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... question. That's not a fair question, because he's already made it clear that this was not an identification based on just one photo, the photo that you are showing him now, or the photo that you were showing when he was interviewed. I don't know when by reference to the previous --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Fine. Fine, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, in the Blagojevic case, transcript page 1404 and 5, in July 2003, that when you entered the school the staircase was on the right. Do you remember?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: And in the Krstic case you stated the same thing, on the 13th of April, 2000, transcript page 2897. Are you sure that the staircase was on the right when you enter the school?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I am sure.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: I think that this happened in 1999. An investigator of the Tribunal took you to that school, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot remember exactly what year it was, but I did go to that school.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go back to open session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Can this possibly be a contested issue at this point?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't know. You're asking me?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I'd object to it as irrelevant, as overly time-consuming, as something that just does not move this trial ahead at all. I mean --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Fauveau, let's bring this to a quick end. Come on, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Sir, you went together with an investigator to that school, didn't you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I don't remember what year it was, but I did go there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Is it fair to say that it was the investigator who took you there? You didn't take him there. He took you there, didn't he?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, one of the investigators with an UNPROFOR APC that was going in front us, and yes, we did go there. It was either UNPROFOR or SFOR. I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: It was an investigator from the Tribunal who showed you the school; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-113 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm going to tell you. I was shown plenty of photographs before that so that I confirm that it wasn't any other schools. When these photographs of this school were brought to me, I confirmed that it was, and then he asked me whether that was that school and I said it was. I went inside. I could confirm it by the way the classroom looked, by where the people were throwing away objects, where they had discarded them, and the blackboard. That's how I understood it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's move to going else now, madam. I think we have a very complete explanation of how he ended up there.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No further questions, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Is there re-examination by any chance, Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sir, basically this means that we're finished with your testimony. Our team here at the Tribunal charged with witnesses and victims will assist you as from now onwards to facilitate your return back home. I can assure you that they are an excellent team, and you don't have to worry about anything. On our part, on behalf of the Tribunal, on behalf of my colleagues here, Judges Prost, Kwon, and Stole, I would like to thank you for having come to this Tribunal once more to give testimony. And on behalf of everyone present here, I wish you a safe journey back home. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We're finished with his testimony but not with the tendering of documents used during his testimony. So the ball is in your court, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the first item would be P02280. That's the transcript of the testimony of -- of P-111 in Blagojevic. The second would be P01908, a photograph of his foot. And then P01910, the frontal injuries. Then P01729, the stairs that -- which access the school. P01730, the stairs inside the school. P01731, the hallway of the first floor of the school. P01732, the panorama of the plateau area, of the dam. P01739, the overflow canal and the plateau. And then P02279, the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: First of all, any objections from any of the Defence teams? Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At this moment I would like to object, Your Honours, about admitting the following exhibits: Photographs 1908 and 1910. I believe that they're not reliable enough in order to be admitted as exhibits. First of all, because none of the photographs shows the face of the person that was wounded. On the other hand, regardless of the fact that this witness confirmed that these are photos of him, that it is a photograph of his chest area and his foot, I believe that that is insufficient, especially in the light of the fact that he was given medical treatment, that there were experts appearing in this case, and that such an assertion of his is not substantiated in any way. I would also finally like to say that we do not know who took the photograph, we don't know the time when the photograph was taken, the place where it was taken, and for that reason it's not possible to establish the chain of possession, how we got a hold of this photograph. So for that reason I believe that at this point those two photographs should not be admitted into evidence. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Is there anyone else of the Defence teams that would like to join Mr. Zivanovic in this objection? All right. Now, any further objections in relation to any of the other documents that the Prosecution seeks to tender? I hear none. Your remarks on Mr. Zivanovic's objection, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE KWON
utterances.text: But before that, can I ask Mr. Zivanovic why he did not bring that issue during his cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We did not question this witness, that is correct. I believe that none of these issues could have been clarified through cross-examination. I'm going to recall the following -- the following: The witness spoke about the mechanism of how he got these wounds that are photographed and, amongst other things, he said that one of those injuries is a -- was caused by fragmentation ammunition. I believe that such an assertion is something that cannot be affirmed or clarified in any way, and it does not make this particular exhibit any more reliable than it is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Mr. President, the witness said those were his injuries. I think he gave us even a time frame, that it was a time after his injuries. That's sufficient foundation in any -- in any court in any land that I'm familiar with. And, yes, I would -- if these kinds of things are going to be in issue I think they need to be discussed in cross-examination so that before a witness leaves if there are issues they can be brought out. But I think this is so fundamental that it's not necessary, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And this is basic to the adversarial system. I mean, you can't have a system of ambush sort of. I mean, let's wait until the Prosecution finishes with its examination-in-chief, states there are no re-examination, and then all of a sudden just say, but you didn't bring evidence as to who the photographer was. It's -- But anyway, I don't want to commit the Trial Chamber before I discuss it with my colleagues. It's not my style. So we'll come back to you on this in a minute, in less than a minute.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Since we are required also to motivate our decisions. Yes, the two documents, namely P01908 and P01910 are being admitted, which basically means that your objection, Mr. Zivanovic, is not being entertained. It's being rejected. The basis for our decision is the following: First, questions were put on examination-in-chief by the -- by Mr. McCloskey to the witness on these two photos, and he testified extensively, inter alia also acknowledging that they were truthfully and faithfully representative of the injuries that he sustained and testified upon. Second is that in the adversarial system if you contested the probative value or authenticity or whatever of these documents, you should have raised this in a timely fashion before or -- the testimony or during the cross-examination. And thirdly, what you raise is ultimately a question of probative value that should be attached to these two documents and that is a matter which will ultimately -- rests with the Trial Chamber and which we will ultimately decide upon at a later stage. But they are being formally admitted into -- into evidence, as are the rest of the -- of the documents that the Prosecution wished to tender. Yes, did I make a mistake somewhere.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: No. I just had one question, Mr. McCloskey. It's a minor point. But on page 20, line 12, you referred to the panorama as P1732, but both of my lists have it as P1737. I just wanted to clarify that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: So do my lists. I -- my eyes must have missed that 7. It wasn't crossed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So it is 1737. Actually, I have the documents that we had yesterday, and two versions of them. In both of them it is 1737. Now, Defence teams. Some of you have made use of documents, some haven't. Do you wish to tender any documents? Mr. Zivanovic? Nothing. Mr. Meek?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic? Madam Nikolic?

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Nikolic Defence would like to tender Exhibit 354 D 50 [as interpreted]. It's the report of the security service of the ABiH army, 2nd Corps. That is all. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the report of the security services. That's where the report that contains supposedly the statement of two persons.

utterances.speaker: MS. NIKOLIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Is there an objection on the part of the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President. This -- this is -- well, beside it being a report of two people, so you have to guess which one they're talking about, it's one of some, I'm not sure, somewhere 10-plus reports or statements of this person, and unless there's a particular reason of relevance, I don't know why we would pick one sort of ambiguous report.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's the one that was used. But anyway, I've taken note of your objection. Let's discuss.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Again, basically for the same reasons that ultimately a matter of what weight the Trial Chamber will need to give to this document, which was put to the witness and he was asked questions about and gave answers upon, so your objection is not sustained. It's rejected. And the document, I lost trace of its number. It's 3 -- what's the number?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: 4D50. Will be 3D4D50.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 3D4D50. All right. I asked you to repeat it because in line 3 on page 24 it's wrong. So for -- it's 3D4D50, okay? Yes. I'm coming to both Prosecution and Defence documents that need to be preserved under seal, but that will be at the end. Mr. Krgovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. KRGOVIC
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau? And Mr. Haynes didn't make use of any documents. So that's it. Now, the following documents or the following exhibits need to be kept under seal. The Defence, Nikolic Defence document, 3D4D50. Prosecution Exhibit P02279. That's the pseudonym sheet. Prosecution Exhibits P01908 and P01910 being the two injury photos. I do not think that any of the other exhibits, Prosecution exhibits, need to be under seal. Correct me if I am wrong. You may come to this even later if you want, Mr. McCloskey. That being done, we can move to the next witness, which is Witness number 54. One moment. I just want to make sure that there are no preliminary matters you wish to raise in relation to this witness. Mr. McCloskey?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: I don't think so. And I would just on a subject that came up last time, I think it was Mr. Krgovic, on fundamental issues relating to the case, I'm always willing to help clarify the charges or the position of the Prosecution. So I remain open to do that, and of course, as you know, I will answer the Judges' questions. I've also on previous trials found at times because of the length of the trials that issues come up such as the one that Mr. Stojanovic brought up, I think very rightly with the Jadar River survivor. He had specific pieces of evidence that he thought would contradict that witness. By the time we get to that evidence, the Jadar River survivor will be long -- well, hopefully not forgotten, but it will be hard to put it in context. So in the past the -- the Chamber in other cases has given the Defence maybe two minutes to -- to say what that evidence is and to -- and to watch for it as it -- as it comes in and the Prosecution two minutes, so that it puts that witness in more of a context, and -- and I have no objection to that. It's -- you know, with seven accused it could get a little long. But anyway, that's just a suggestion to help make more sense out of these witnesses, because these witnesses are part of a bigger puzzle and they're not always clear when -- when we just put them on in the traditional fashion where they fit.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I personally think that's a good piece of food for thought. We'll discuss it amongst ourselves during one of the breaks and come back to you, but I thank you for the suggestion. And if you have any off-the-cuff comments now, perhaps that would help us even more. Yes, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Your Honours. Thank you very much. I believe that our Defence team has received a suggestion from Mr. McCloskey which is very important for us as a guideline as to how to cross-examine future witnesses. However, my impression is that what Mr. McCloskey has said today is directly connected with certain parts of the indictment, and it deals with the number of people who suffered, who were killed or were wounded and whose suffering represents a crime, and that is in direct connection with the Article 36 of the indictment. I come from a continental system, and I believe that we should have a discussion with the Prosecution in order to curtail our cross-examination. The way I see it, people who were from the army of BiH should not make part of the indictment, and counting the number of dead people would lead us a long way and would lead us off the track when it comes to the number of dead and wounded.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Josse.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Your Honour, our only observation is that before the Chamber perhaps make any decisions about my learned friend's very interesting and helpful suggestion, could the Defence be given a little bit of time to discuss it amongst ourselves and perhaps indeed discuss it with Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's a very wise situation. As you may have noticed, we didn't jump to any conclusions ourselves, and I ask for your remarks in any case, because I don't think we should even start discussing it unless we have heard your remarks on it.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Off-the-cuff and then we'll see later. Yes. Any further remarks? Yes. All right. Now, as regards this witness, we're talking of Witness number 54; correct? And you require the whole of today, I take it, to finish your examination-in-chief?

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: That's -- that's the plan. Again, we're getting a little quicker with the new -- new system, and -- but I better let Mr. Nicholls speak for the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. In the meantime, I do not have -- we do not have an indication of the anticipated time required by the Defence for cross-examination. Perhaps at the first break you could organise yourselves and give us a first indication of the time -- time required. The other thing I wanted to make sure of is that we agree on the identification of the protective measures that we have already decided upon. The decision refers back -- goes back to a couple of -- a day, a day ago? No. Yesterday. Yes. And he has a pseudonym which will be 118, 118, and facial -- and facial distortion only. Pseudonym and facial distortion. All right. So we can admit the witness now. I'll explain to him the position. And, Madam Usher, have you explained to him why we are starting with his testimony -- I'll explain to him. Don't explain anything. I'll explain it to him.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. President, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: This is a 92 witness, so I'll be reading a summary. There won't be a full -- unfortunately, there won't be a full direct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, this is why I asked Mr. McCloskey whether it's correct that you require two hours and 25 minutes for -- for the direct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, that's not, Your Honour. I think that was probably written down if it had been a full live witness. It will not be nearly that long on my part.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Great news.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good morning to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On behalf of the Tribunal, I wish to welcome you to this Tribunal. You are one other witness in this trial dealing with the July 1995 Srebrenica events. You are a Prosecution witness. We know that you have testified in Krstic already and, therefore, you should be familiar with our procedure. Madam Usher who is standing next to you is going to happened to you the text of a solemn, formal -- solemn declaration which you need to confirm to us; namely, that in the course of your testimony you will be speaking the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth. Madam Usher, please. And, Witness, could you kindly read that solemn declaration aloud, and that would be your undertaking with us that you will testify the truth.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please make yourself comfortable.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls will be the officer on the Prosecution team that will put to you some questions. You will not be required to go through the entire events as you did in Krstic. We have admitted the transcript of your testimony in Krstic to be valid also for the purpose of this trial. A lot of time has passed under the bridges since you testified in Krstic, so the first thing that will happen is that Mr. Nicholls will read out a brief summary of your testimony in that case, and then he will proceed with some questions to you. After that, you will be cross-examined by the seven Defence teams. I will introduce each team to you as we go along. The Prosecution on your behalf asked that you will be granted some protective measures for the duration of your testimony here. We have consulted not only the Prosecution on this but also the Defence teams, and all the Defence teams were very cooperative and agreed with the Prosecution request that you be granted these protective measures. The first of these protective measures is that in order to protect, hide your identity, no one will refer to you by your name here. We will refer to you by a number, and in the records of this case you are going to be known as Prosecution Witness PW-118. The other protective measure that the Prosecution asked for, the Defence teams agreed to, and which we are granting is that no one will be able to view your face from outside the walls of this courtroom. You know that the proceedings are transmitted live and sometimes with a delay to various TV stations. They can also be followed on computer, on the internet. In order to make sure that no one can recognise you, your face will not be shown. Instead, if you look at your screen in front of you and if the cameras focus on you, you will immediately see how you are going to it appear to the general public that will be viewing these proceedings from outside. And could we focus on the witness. Could we have the camera focus on the witness. Yes. That's how you will appear. In other words, a number of coloured squares, which you can see on your screen. Is that to your satisfaction, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I'm very satisfied. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. I can now safely hand you over to Mr. Nicholls. He will first proceed with the reading out of the summary. We will have a break at 10.30, Mr. Nicholls. Before he starts, sir, I wish to explain to you that you were kept in the room outside in the corridor here waiting for an hour and a quarter, or even move, not capriciously. We were still hearing the testimony of another witness, which only finished about 15 minutes ago, and then we needed to deal with and finalise some procedural matters. That's the reason why you were kept waiting. I'm sure you understand.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand, and it's not a problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls, he's all yours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Good morning, sir. Thank you very much for coming today.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: First I need to show the witness the pseudonym sheet. If I could have the assistance of the usher. This is P02281, which will be under seal, and if you could show it to my colleagues afterwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at that. Do not read what -- the name on the sheet out loud, but could you please confirm that your name is written there under PW-118?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Show it to Mr. Zivanovic, please. Okay. That satisfies, I suppose. Yes. That will be admitted, of course, in due course, and with the understanding that it's one of the documents that will be kept under seal.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, I'm now going to read a brief summary of your evidence in the Krstic trial. The witness was born in 1964. He is a Muslim by faith. The witness grew up in and around the town of Srebrenica. Before the war, he worked as a machine operator at the bauxite mine company in Srebrenica. On the 11th of July, 1995, the witness was at home at his house in Srebrenica. He suffered from a leg injury which he had received at the beginning of the war. That day, the witness decided to go to Potocari with his family. The witness went to Potocari because he was afraid that he would be killed by the advancing Serb army if he stayed in his house. The witness believed that as he had been wounded, DutchBat would offer him some protection. At Potocari there was a huge crowd of people and no accommodation. At around noon, the witness and his family entered the bus compound in Potocari. This was a building used for maintenance of buses. The witness and his family found space in a corner of the building, and he stayed in the bus compound the entire day. His wife went to her parents' house which was nearby to get some food. She spoke to her father while she was there. This was the last time that she ever saw her father. The evening in the bus compound was horrible. The people could hear powerful detonations of shells which the witness believed came from shelling of the town centre and the surrounding area. There was not enough space in the bus compound. It was crowded. Children were crying, and mothers had to try to bring in hay for the children to sleep on. There was not enough food. People needed to go to the toilet. And the witness couldn't sleep at all that night because he was in a sitting position. By morning, 12th of July, there was mounting panic in the bus compound. Serb soldiers entered the bus compound, and they behaved decently. These soldiers checked the documents of men in the compound. The witness showed his identification to the soldiers and they asked him why he was there. He told them he was wounded, and they accepted this answer. Towards dusk, the people in the compound heard that men were being separated. This frightened the witness. The witness decided to try to hide. He and his family went and hid in one of several broken-down buses which were in front of the bus compound. The witness spent the night of 12 July in this broken bus. He spent all night on the bus and didn't leave because one could hear screams, loud screams of women and children. It was beyond description. The witness could hear people screaming things like, "Let me go. Don't. Please, let me be. Leave me alone." Women were crying and screaming and asking for help. The next morning, 13 July, at dawn the witness decided that he and his family had to leave. His wife left first to get some water from a house across the street. She came back and told the witness that she'd seen a lot of blood on the ground floor of the house. The witness was shaken, but he picked up his child and headed for the group at the exit where two UN APCs were parked. At this point, the witness's mother was also with him. The witness found himself in an even bigger crowd of people who were all trying to get out. There were women, children, and a few men. It took a long time, but the witness finally got through the crowd to the APCs. He was still carrying his child. At the APCs, the witness saw UN soldiers holding hands to control the movement of the crowd toward the buses. The witness also saw Serb soldiers who had already reached the buses move away for a moment as if they had been called away by someone. When the soldiers left for a moment, the witness boarded a bus and hid on the floor from the Serb soldiers. He hid because he was afraid that if the soldiers saw him that he would be separated as they had done to other men. The bus was extremely overcrowded, and finally left in the direction of Bratunac. The bus went from Potocari to Bratunac, Glogova, Kravica, Konjevic Polje, Nova Kasaba, Milici, Vlasenica, Tisca, and finally stopped in Luke. While passing through Kravica, the witness heard women and children on the bus crying and shouting because of what they saw outside. The witness looked outside and saw men lying to the left and right of the bus who did not seem to be moving. He also saw about 50 men who appeared to be captured. These prisoners had their hands behind their necks. The prisoners were in civilian clothes and looked horrified. Nearby there were armed Serb soldiers. On the way to Luke, the bus was stopped several times and checked for men. The bus driver was very decent and said there were only women and children on the bus. At times the front and rear doors of the bus were opened to be checked but no one saw the witness hiding. At Luke the bus stopped and everyone got off. The witness was still carrying his five-year-old child. The bus driver told people to proceed on foot from this point. After a few steps, the witness saw several Serb soldiers. One of the soldiers told the witness, "Give your child to your wife and you come with us." The witness handed the child to his wife. He believed that he would never see the child again, so he tried to say something, but he couldn't speak. He didn't have time. The Serb soldier pushed him with a rifle and said, "Move on." The soldier asked a man in camouflage trouser and a sweater, "Major, what do we do with him?" And the major pointed the way that they should go down the road. The soldier leading the witness away turned down the road and asked him, "Did you work for bauxite?" And it turned out that the witness and the Serb soldier recognised each other, as they had both worked for bauxite. Your Honours, I have about -- I'm about a little bit more than halfway through, so I don't know if you want to break now or -- I probably won't finish in the next two minutes or so.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do I have the okay of the technicians and interpreters to on for the next five, six, seven minutes and then we'll have a 30-minute break after that?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thumbs up. Okay. All right. Then carry on and finish it and we'll have the break immediately after.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: They continued down the road as indicated by the major and arrived at the Luke school. The time was approximately 10.00 a.m. In front of the Luke school the witness recognised a prisoner with his hands tied behind his back, Abdul Kadir, a young lab technician, a medical technician from the hospital in Srebrenica. In his Krstic testimony the witness was shown a series of photos which he recognised to be the school building where he was held captive in Luke on 13 July 1995. These were P02103 at page 20, a panorama shot of the school and the road. P01765, a photo of the area outside the school, and I'll ask to admit that at the end today. P01766, another photo of outside the school where the prisoners sat under a tree. I'll ask to admit that photo as well. And P01767 a photograph of the classroom inside the school where the prisoner was held and I'll ask to admit that. Immediately after arriving at the school the witness's hands were tied behind his back with shoelaces. There was one soldier there who only answered a military telephone set up in the stairway. This soldier was Zeljko by the other soldiers, and he would speak on the phone and say, "Yes, sir, I'll do that. I'll tell them." The witness sat for most of the day outside the school with Abdul Kadir. Throughout the day the witness observed prisoners continuously being brought to the school. He could hear trucks and buses coming and going as the number of prisoners increased. Eventually, there were 22 prisoners being held in front of the Luke school. Serb soldiers came and went during this time. Many of them threatened the prisoners but the prisoners were not beaten. A Serb soldier Stanimir asked the witness if he knew a Serb soldier named Spomenko Garic, who also worked at bauxite. The witness replied that he did know Garic from work. Stanimir told the witness that Garic was the commander of a special intervention unit that was currently in the field in Kravica and said that Garic would probably be by the school later in the evening. Later towards the evening the Serb soldiers brought a very pretty Muslim girl of about 17 to the school to try to identify some of the prisoners. The soldiers called her Turkish Girl, told her she was pretty, and took her into the school. Later, the witness heard a female screaming in the school, "Let me go. Don't touch me." That night at about 9.00 p.m. approximately, the 22 prisoners were brought into the school. As they were brought into the school, they were searched and robbed of their money and valuables by the Serb soldiers. In a classroom in the school, the prisoners were bound with telephone wire. Their hands were tied behind their backs. The prisoners were ordered to sit on the floor in a corner of the classroom and were guarded by a soldier with a rifle. Soon Spomenko Garic arrived. He asked, "Who is from bauxite here?" The witness replied, and Garic asked the witness what he was doing there. The witness replied that he had been wounded, that he had gone to Potocari, and that he had been taken into custody and brought to the school. Garic replied, "Well, this war hasn't been very good to you or us, but what can we do? Right. Very well. See you tomorrow." He gave the witness a friendly pat on the soldier and left. Garic was dressed in coveralls and had a handkerchief tied around his head. Immediately after he left Serb troops came into the classroom. They were dressed in a similar fashion to Garic. The guard asked them, "How did you fare in Kravica?" And they replied, "Great. We've finish with the balijas." These soldiers then began to question and beat the prisoners. Beatings were brutal. With each question, for example, how many Serbs did you kill, a blow would fall. Prisoners with beaten on their heads with rifles. They were kicked in the chest. An old man being beaten dropped his metal cane and a soldier picked it up and beat him with it. One of the soldiers took a flag which had been taken from mosque and began to beat the witness and other prisoners with the metal rod of the flag. He asked questions about the flag and then beat the prisoners whatever their answer may be. The witness was scarred above his right eye and his face was covered with blood. He was kicked to the floor. The beatings lasted about half an hour. The prisoners were covered in blood. The accents of the soldiers inflicting the beatings was a normal accent like that of the people of Srebrenica. The soldiers conducting the beatings left and a new group of five or six soldiers entered the building. The prisoners were ordered to stand against the wall. Some of them could not stand. The prisoners were then ordered out of the school and into a truck. There was a platform set up on the stairs outside the school which led into the bed of the truck. A soldier at the stairs told the prisoners that they were going to a military prison and that it would be quite nice there. This soldier said, "Don't be afraid. Everything will be all right." The prisoners were ordered to sit on the right-hand bench of the truck and were told to keep the other bench free. Two soldiers loaded the beaten prisoners who could not walk into the bed of the truck. They threw the prisoners into the back of the truck and piled them in a heap. There was no tarpaulin on the truck. Four soldiers then took the free right-hand bench and three got into the cab of the truck. The truck took the road towards Vlasenica. Just at the entry of the town of Vlasenica on a lit street the truck turned left onto a dirt road. At some point the truck reached a small stream or brook and stopped briefly. A Serb soldier in the bed of the truck banged with his fist on the roof of the cab and above the driver and said, "Not here. Take them up there where they took the people before." He said it very loudly and it was quite clear. The driver understood him and the truck proceeded. During the journey, the witness had been trying to loosen the telephone wire binding his hands by working it against a screw attached to the frame of the truck. He succeeded in loosening it, although he could not undo the knot. The truck stopped as it was going up a hill. There was a pasture and a partly demolished house there. The truck stopped near the house and turned off its engine although the lights remained on. The four soldiers got off the back of the truck. The three soldiers got out of the cabin. The three soldiers from the cabin were opposite from where the witness was sitting on the other side of the truck. One of the four soldiers from the back of the truck went over to front where the three soldiers from the cab were standing. The three remaining soldiers at the back of the truck immediately starting killing the prisoners. They threw the prisoners off the back of the truck and began shooting them. Two men tried to escape. They jumped off the truck and ran about 20 metres before they were shot down. The witness managed to free one of his hands. He jumped off the truck, putting the truck between himself and the soldiers and he ran. The soldiers fired at him. It was night-time and the soldiers had to fire over the truck. The witness managed to get to the edge of the forest, and he fell and rolled down a steep slope and reached a brook at the bottom. He could still hear gun-fire. The witness remained there until dawn the next day. At dawn the witness set out. After seven days, approximately, he met some fellow Muslims who were also trying to escape. After a great deal of intense hunger, hardship, and a Serb army ambush, the witness manned to reach the free territory on 27 July 1995. That concludes my summary.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Nicholls, and I thank all the staff for their patience and cooperation. We'll have a 30-minute break starting from now. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: With some luck, Witness, we may be able to finish with your testimony today. Mr. Nicholls, do you have any further questions or, rather, do you have questions for your witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I do have questions on a few topics, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead then.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Any time you need to go into private session, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, you spent your whole life in the Srebrenica area up to 1995 except for compulsory JNA service in Kosovo in 1984; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: At the beginning of the war, were you ever in a village guard unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes. I have to clarify a little bit here. When the war came to Srebrenica, the people of Srebrenica organised in such a way that they protected their villages. Since I could not live in my house at the beginning of the war, my house was among Serb houses. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: May I request a redaction of the school friend's name.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Madam Usher -- registrar.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: What period --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's line 7, I suggest, to line 10.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suggest -- I suppose we will need to draw -- once this has happened, we need to draw the witness's attention. Witness, look at me. It often happens that in spite of every effort we make to protect your identity, to hide it, then mistakes are made. You made the first one today by mentioning the name of someone, and that in itself could lead to other people being able to identify you. So be careful when you are testifying not to mention names or places which are so intimately connected or related to you that anyone who would be following the proceedings would be in a position to identify your -- you as a witness today. All right?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for that instruction, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes. Go ahead, Mr. Nicholls, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you tell me what period of time approximately you were a village guard?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: From the 17th of April until I was wounded on the 14th of May, 1992. Perhaps it's not that precise time period, but it's more or less that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And can you describe what happened to you on the 14th of May, 1992, how you were injured, and what the nature of the injury was.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: On the 14th of May, 1992, that evening I was on guard duty. During the morning I was sitting in front of my school friend's house when that place was shelled. A shell that fell in the immediate vicinity wounded me and another guy and it killed one woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. From 17th of April, 1992, until you were injured, did you actually take part in any combat?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: No. At the time, the Serbs were controlling the town. People who lived in the Muslim villages just organised guard shifts around their villages. There were no military conflicts at that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Now, after you were injured in May 1992, and the fall of Srebrenica in July 1995, did you take part in any combat during that period of time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: No, I didn't participate in it afterwards. My healing process was very specific. It took a while. I spent a long time using two crutches in order to move around. I have to also add that the hospital wasn't adequate. There were no medicines. In the beginning we had whatever people had on them. So you could borrow some medicines, but later on there were no medicines.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. I would like one clarification from Mr. Nicholls, if possible. Here I'm reading the transcript that at the time the Serbs were controlling the town. I would like to know whether he's referring to Srebrenica, to Bratunac, what specific.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In answering that, just decide for yourself whether we need to go into private session or not.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I would request private session, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thought so. So let's go to private session for a while, please. And thank you, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: A moment ago you referred to the hospital being inadequate. Are you referring to the hospital in Srebrenica?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes. Just as I said before. Serb soldiers or Serbs were looting everything they could get their hands on in Srebrenica, including the hospital. Many items from the hospital, medicines, were looted and taken in an unknown direction out of Srebrenica. The hospital was not functioning. After a while, after two or three months, a military hospital or a field hospital was set up in Srebrenica headed by Dr. Nijaz.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Now, during the time period before the fall of Srebrenica, after the start of the war, were you aware of the population of Srebrenica increasing as people came into Srebrenica from surrounding villages?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. The number of people in Srebrenica increased on a daily basis because Serbs or Serb soldiers were attacking Muslim settlements, and the Muslim population was expelled from neighbouring villages around Srebrenica and were being pushed into the town of Srebrenica itself. Later, the Muslim people were in complete control of the town of Srebrenica after an action that took place in Potocari when they definitely pushed back Serbian soldiers in an ambush that was set up in Potocari.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. I want you to very briefly please describe the living conditions in Srebrenica, 1993, 1994, 1995, in terms of food, you've already spoken about medicine, but water and housing space for these -- for the population as it increased.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: It was terrible in Srebrenica in terms of food, clothing, footwear. Medical supplies were most needed, because from day to day the number of wounded people was ever-greater, and they needed medical supplies, medicines and other equipment, and it wasn't available. People had to actively look for food. There was no food. And if you wish, I can describe that separately. All in all, the overall situation was terrible. There was no water. Electricity was cut off, telephone lines also. There was no food. In one word, you could describe it as horrific.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You've already told us about how you were injured by shelling. Briefly can you tell me how the shelling of Srebrenica affected life for the inhabitants, how it affected their psychological state.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: The daily shelling of the town made life more difficult for the people who were pushed into the town and forced to use all available accommodation for their families. There were often dead people lying in the streets because of the shelling. We all knew, those of us who lived in Srebrenica, that up to 1.000 shells fell every day in such a small town. Serb artillery was occupying the elevations around the town, so it was very simple to hit the targets that they wanted to hit. I must mention once again Dr. -- Dr. Nijaz whom I mentioned before. He was hit by an air -- by a bomb dropped from the air. Actually, he was killed by a bomb that was dropped from the air. When I mention aerial bombardment, this was also used against the suffering population of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour. Your Honour, could the witness specify which period he means.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. A very legitimate question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could you --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which period of time are you specifically referring to now?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That was in early 1993 and in late 1992. I believe that that was a very, very difficult period, and so what I'm talking about now relates to that period.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... that it's better if we move nearer to 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Yes. Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I want to talk to you now about something you testified to in Krstic, which is the separations at Potocari. And you previously have described the separation of men you saw as you waited to try to board the bus. Do you remember making a sketch of that scene during your interview with the OTP in January 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, I do. It still lingers in my memory what I could see on that day.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session while I ask for P02282 to be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session --

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: -- placed in e-court.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- for a short while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You were able to get on the bus in Potocari with your wife, your mother, and your daughter. Did your brother go with you on the bus? Was he able to get on any bus with you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: No. My brother went together with other people across the forest.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: When was the last time you saw your brother?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: I saw him before the fall of Srebrenica. Maybe a few days before that. I can't remember exactly. But in any case, it was immediately before the fall of Srebrenica.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
