utterances.text: One question about when you got off the bus in Luke with your family. Were you able to see if what happened with the bus that you had been on? Did it stay there? Did it go away? What did the bus do?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: The bus turned and went back in the same direction. I suppose that it went to pick up the next group of people.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd now like to show the witness, on another topic, sir, 02103, page 21. That's a photo. It does not need to be in private session.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Unfortunately, that's not in colour. We can show the witness the photo in colour, which I would refer if that's acceptable to the Chamber. It's the same photo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Chamber would prefer it.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sir, this is a photo which I showed you when we met the other day; isn't that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that's right. That is the photo that I have already seen.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Please just tell me -- well, do you recognise the place in the photograph?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, I do. This is the school where people were brought to. Actually, they were brought to the area in front of the school, and later on they were taken into the school. There were two trees here, one of them closer to the school and the other one a bit further from the school, and under that latter I found the first person who had been brought in, and I sat down close to him. And later on, all the people were sitting under that tree, and that was during the day. When the evening came, they were taken into the school.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Thank you. And I think that's clear, you're referring to the tree in the foreground on the right-hand side of the photo.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. That's the tree.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And just to be absolutely clear, this is the same school that you testified about in Krstic, the one I recounted in the summary earlier today?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could we go into private session now, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Zivanovic who is defending Colonel Popovic will now cross-examine you. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good morning, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Good morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were wounded in 1992; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, I was wounded in 1992 on the 14th of May.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: After that, up to July 1995 were you ever called up to join the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, I was, but my answer was that I could not participate in fighting, and this was verified by them when they sent me for a medical check-up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, your health condition was such that you could not, for that reason, join the army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: That's correct. I was wounded in my right lower leg, and I still have a 1 centimetre by 1.5 centimetre shrapnel in my leg. We have a photo of that, and if you wish it can be shown to you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Were you also called to join the TO since you were not capable of joining the army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: No, nobody called me into the TO or the civilian protection.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: What about the work obligation? Did you need to do that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: No, I didn't. Because I was proclaimed unfit for any such activity.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You remember --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can we please go into private session, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, let's go into private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. We are in open session. And I suppose you need to repeat your question, because I interrupted you the way I did.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I will repeat my question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said that immediately when you jumped off the truck they immediately opened fire at you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that is what I said. That is what I said, because I could hear firing. When they were executing people, they were using short bursts of fire. The minute I jumped off the truck, somebody from the left side of the truck or something -- I heard somebody say, "He's escaping, fuck his balija mother." And then there was firing. So all I could hear was that there was firing in my -- there was firing in my direction. They wanted to hit me. This is normal.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please tell me whether it's normal also that they would chase after you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: I said in my previous sentence that I don't know that -- whether they ran around the truck and started to run after me in the direction that I was going in. Probably they did, because I hear that the bursts of fire were quite close to me. I described in another situation in more detail what I believed probably could have happened. When I reached the actual wood, the slope was even more steep, so I had to roll down the -- on the ground.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You were quite tired. How were you able to then run and roll down the slope?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that is a good question, but when a person is in such a life-threatening situation, then it is very difficult, but things inexplicably happen and you just find yourself able to do things that you normally wouldn't be able to do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's given you his answer. But what is worrying me is the speed again. I can -- I am really feeling sorry for the interpreters. It's both of you, and I'm not distinguishing between one or the other today. But you're simply not allowing -- not even a split second. He's anticipating your questions. You are questioning him again before he's even answered fully. It can't go on like this.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation], Your Honours, I apologise. I made a mistake, I'm not wearing headphones. I should have done that in this case. But I have completed my cross-examination of this witness in any case, so I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. I understand the Beara Defence team had required 20 minutes. Yes, Mr. Meek.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: That's correct, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Meek is defending, together with Mr. Ostojic, Colonel Beara in this case, and he's going to cross-examine you next.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. How are you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Good day. How are you? Are you doing all right?

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: I'm doing fine. I just have a few questions, and I'd just ask you, if you could, listen to them and answer as succinctly as you can so we can move on and get done with this ordeal. Okay?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes. I agree. Please go ahead. Put your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Witness, am I correct that the late morning of the 12th of July that the soldiers who asked you for your identification treated you decently and correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: When I said correctly, properly, there was no beating up, they didn't provoke us, the soldiers who were walking around in the usual way, between women and children, and when they came up to a man they would ask for his identification, what his name was, can he give them their correct name. Then they would also ask about the participation of or in the army in the latest events in Srebrenica. This is what happened when they came up to me. They asked me what my name was, did I have a personal ID card.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And, Witness, you told these soldiers on the 12th of July that you had been wounded. Did they ask you first why you were there, correct, yes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, I told them --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You're anticipating my questions and I'm anticipating your answers. You told them that you had been wounded and they said fine; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: They moved on to the next person and they just continued on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: You already anticipated one of my questions. They didn't harm you. They didn't mistreat you. And as soon as they had completed their questioning you were left alone. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: These were -- these were military police officers; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: I assume that it was a group of soldiers who had been given a special assignment. That is my opinion. To go inside, identify people, perhaps. And they were different from the local soldiers by their accent. In Bosnia, Serbia, there are different accents, and we can, when we listen to one another, determine that a person is from such-and-such an area. I, at that point, was able to see that they were from a different area.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And again, I want to -- I don't want to put it on the e-court, but you gave a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor here on 24 January 1996. Do you recall that statement? In that statement, you just stated that it was a special unit of the military police of the Chetnik forces in the area; correct? Now --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: These were just my assumptions. As I said, they were different from the regular soldiers, and I asserted that there were such groups in the army. There were special police units or special purpose units. This was the basis for my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Can you just roughly tell me how large of a group these military police -- how large a group was it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: What I saw was that they moved in twos and threes, in two and three groups that I was able to see, in the facility where I was. It's possible that there were more of them outside. I couldn't see the entire area. There were a lot of people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: So would it be fair to say that you saw 10 to 12, 15 to 20 of these soldiers, military police, in different groups? That's what I'm trying to get at.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: It's correct that two people came up to me. Further off, I could see a group of three people who were looking at people and checking their IDs, IDs of two other men. There were groups of two or three of these men, and they were wandering around amongst the people, speaking to them, and then they left in a regular way.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. And I take it that the two military police officers who questioned you had an accent which you believed came from Montenegro; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, yes. That is correct. That was my conclusion. The way they spoke made me think that they spoke in a Montenegrin accent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, the other members of the military police who you saw among the crowd asking for ID, you didn't hear them speak, did you, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: No, I didn't hear them. All I saw is was that they wore the same uniforms as these other people. And when we're talking about the uniform, they were different from the regular Serb army uniforms. They seemed to be of better quality. They were finer than the regular Serb army uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: And of the two military police officers who questioned you and asked for your identity, did both of them have this accent or only one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: One of them talked to me and the other one didn't speak to me at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Now, you mentioned in your testimony which you gave in a previous proceeding here, Witness, about an individual by the name of --

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Maybe we should go into closed session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, Mr. Meek. Let's go into private session for a while, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Would you like me to repeat the question?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: There is no need. It's a person who was taken away. It's true that later I have found out from the women who were there that they had mentioned his name. I'm not going to mention his name. He was taken away. He was taken off in an unknown direction. When I reached the free territory, for a while there was nothing that was known about him. Later he was exchanged, probably interrogated. People probably know what happened with him in the course of his processing.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness, my final question is: You never saw this group of military police officers after the 12th, that day in Potocari. Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: No, I didn't meet people in such uniforms, no.

utterances.speaker: MR. MEEK
utterances.text: Thank you very much. I have no further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. I think, Usher, you can escort the witness out. In the meantime, there are two very brief matters I'd like to refer you to. The first one, Mr. McCloskey, I am referring you to the matter relating to your motion and then responses of a second motion relating to a request to amend the witness list and 65 ter witness list and 65 ter exhibit list. Yes, exactly. He knows exactly what I'm talking about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have completed our deliberations on this matter, and in relation to your request for the addition of approximately 230 exhibits, we have come to the conclusion that although you seemingly provide in your first motion detailed justification for adding approximately 230 exhibits to your Prosecution list; however, you do not provide similar explanation with respect to the additional 31 exhibits which you also seek to the Prosecution exhibit list, and you do not identify, as a result, which of the 261 exhibits listed in Annex B attached to the first motion are those approximately, using your own words, approximately 230 exhibits. In other words, we are not in a position to identify those 31 -- 31 exhibits. I think you need to look into this and thus it will help us avoiding having to give two decisions instead of one. If you can look into this as soon as possible, we would be in a position to hand down our decision immediately after. So I think you understand what I mean. I mean, it's -- you seek to admit 261, but it's not clear exactly which are the 230 and which are the 31, and that we need to know. The other thing is this: Again yesterday you filed another motion for protective measures, referring to witnesses due to give evidence in the course of this month we've just started today. One of these witnesses, namely the one with 65 ter number 40, is, according to my calculations, due to start to testify probably early next week. So it will be helpful if at least in relation to this witness the Defence teams could give us their position possibly by tomorrow, so that would enable us to decide the matter by Friday. And if that would be the case, then you can proceed with bringing the witness on -- as soon as possible next week. All right? So I trust that one of you will deal -- deal with this and feed us back. All right. We'll have a 30-minute break. Mr. Lazarevic, I think that you will be taking the witness for cross-examination, and then I think it's you. Can you possibly see if it's possible for both of you to finish in 45 minutes? Of course we are not forcing you to, but try.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, who is representing --

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'd like to say to you that I won't be able to finish in 45 minutes. It's Mr. Lazarevic who will take on from me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right, So, Mr. Lazarevic, please start your cross-examination. Mr. Lazarevic is representing accused Borovcanin in this case. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let us just clarify one mistake. Yesterday from our learned friend Nicholls, who represents the Prosecution here, we received the so-called supplemental information sheet with some new information informing the Defence teams of what he had learned during your proofing, and in that document we found a sentence which I would like to clarify with you. It says here, and I shall read it in English, it will be translated to you: [In English] "After reaching Muslim-held territory, the witness served in the 286th Brigade in traffic administration. He did not take part in combat." [Interpretation] In order to speed things up, I'm going to put simple questions to you to which you can answer by yes or no. First of all, did you say this to Mr. Nicholls during your proofing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: I have to explain one thing. It is correct that I said this. The sentence is correct, but I have to explain why I found myself in that unit that had been set up in the place called Stupari. This was for my on subsistence. I was not a member of any unit. I did not receive any money or any bare essentials. My family had to live on something. When I arrived in that unit, I explained my situation. I told them I was awaiting surgery, that I could not perform any tasks in the unit, but they told me that my profession entitled me to performing some tasks and doing some jobs that are tied to the office, that were office work, and that's how I accepted the position. But I stayed there for a very brief time. Very soon after that I underwent surgery in the hospital for orthopaedic surgery in Tuzla.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Okay. I understand your reasons. I understand everything you have just said. But can you please specify the period this happened when you were a member of the 286th Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: It was the 286th Brigade, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because we're doing exactly what we had previously. Witness, you -- actually, you started. Mr. Lazarevic, he hadn't even finished his answer. You already had started your next question. You were already continuing to talk while Mr. Lazarevic was still putting a new question. We can't go on like this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I understand. I apologise. I shall wait. I just wanted to economise on time but of course it's better to wait for the interpreters.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe it would be good, sir, that you look at the screen in front of you. You will see the transcript of the words that are being said, and when you see the line has stopped moving, you will know when to start answering. I would like to deal with a person whom you mentioned during your testimony in answering my learned friend Meek's question, and you mentioned that person in the Krstic case as well?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. But that was in private session to my recollection as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: No. I believe that is not the person I at the time intend to refer to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Then go ahead.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: (redacted)and we move to private session, please, immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Witness, what is the meaning of the word "sehid"? Can you explain to the Trial Chamber?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: This is a very difficult question for me. I really don't know the meaning of that word.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: However, you must have heard that word because you hail from Srebrenica, from Bosnia. I'm sure you must have heard the word "sehid" used many times.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, I heard it, I read it. But I can't explain what it means.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If I were to put it to you that "sehid" is most commonly used in terms of a fighter who died for the Muslim religion, would you say agree with that definition of "sehid"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: You are making me say something that I don't know. I've already told you, I don't know the meaning of the word.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... and if I can please -- again, you are moving a little bit too fast and not allowing for a pause between question and answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Let's try and make an effort to avoid any more warnings from the Trial Chamber. You make a pause and I'll make a pause. Let's both of us be patient. Can we go back to Potocari and the 12th of July. On page 1253 of the Krstic transcript, in pages [as interpreted] 9 and 10, you stated about the 12th of July: "[In English] From those women and men who wanted to go out, to leave on that 20th [sic], we heard that men were being separated." [Interpretation] Can you please answer by saying yes or no? Does the Krstic transcript reflect what you said at the time?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: I am not sure that I understand you and I didn't understand the quote. Can you repeat the quote?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You spoke about what you heard about the separation of men from women on the 12th of July in Potocari. And in English the sentence reads as follows: "[In English] Those women and men who wanted to go out to leave on that 20th [sic], we heard that men were being separated." I'm sorry, I said 12th. I apologise. Instead of 20th, of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let me -- one moment. And this is line --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: It says 12th, actually.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: On page 1253. One moment. Let me just make sure that isolated from the rest of the text. Yes. Go ahead. I think you need to read the whole answer. Let me help you a little bit.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. Maybe it would be --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, look at me. You remember I referred earlier on to your testimony in Krstic. We have it all here, and I'm going to read a very short part on which Mr. Lazarevic would like to question you. In Krstic, you were asked the following question: "How long did you stay inside the bus compound on July the 12th?" And according to the transcript, you answered as follows: "Towards the dusk, in late afternoon, from those women and men who wanted to go out, to leave on that 12th, we heard that men were being separated, and that frightened me, so that naturally I tried to find some safety, to find a safer place where I wouldn't be noticed." This is the extract from your testimony that Mr. Lazarevic is interested in. So now you can proceed with your question, Mr. Lazarevic.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Since you have now been presented with that section of the transcript, is what you stated then absolutely correct and accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, it's absolutely correct and accurate. This was at the time I was in the transportation facility. They maintained those buses. I wasn't able to see over there, but I heard it. That's why I got scared, and I had to hide in a more secure place.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So you personally did not see this on the 12th, but you heard about it; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Actually, I heard from the people that those men were being separated and that -- and later I had the opportunity to see that, but this was that first contact when I heard of it. Later I had the opportunity to see how those groups of Serbian soldiers were entering amongst the people. And again that evening I heard moaning and screams of those people whom they were taking away.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I asked you, I think, I put a very clear question to you. We're talking about the 12th. On the 12th, did you see for yourself this or did you find that out from others? We're talking about the 12th.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: On the 12th, I was not able to see that because I was inside the building.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much. And the first time you saw that was on the 13th when you also approached the two Dutch combat vehicles?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. You could see it from that location. You could see them separating people to the left, and all of those who were in front of me were separated to the left towards that house which I already described.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: You told us that on the 12th of July you were in what we called that facility here as the bus maintenance depot. You were inside this bus maintenance depot. The entire depot and the area in front of it were full of refugees. Is that an exact description of that place where you were on the 12th?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. It was overbooked. People were in front. There were many people there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And since there was a site visit made by the Trial Chamber so that they could familiarise themselves with the area, and we also toured the area, would you be able to say whether the depot facility where you were was about 150 metres away from the road? There is an area of about 150 metres between the depot and the road. Would that be accurate?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: I couldn't give you an exact distance. I really wouldn't be able to tell you what that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, all right. Thank you. It's not really that essential. Since you were inside the depot and there were refugees between you and the road, you were unable to see on the 12th what was going on up on the road where the buses were; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: I was inside the building. I already explained that I wasn't able to see from inside the building. Probably even if I were in front of the building it would have been hard to see because of the mass of people that was there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would now like for us to look at the statement that you gave to the Prosecutors of this Tribunal on the 24th of January, 1996. This is Exhibit 5D93. Do you recall in January 1996 speaking with representatives of the Prosecutor's office of this Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: We have some reason to be worried about the identity of the witness. Perhaps -- I don't know whether this is broadcasted -- no, it's not. Okay then.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you talked about the Prosecutors of The Hague Tribunal, I assume that they treated you professionally and they recorded your words correctly and exactly. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And you had the opportunity to see your statement during the proofing with Mr. Nicholls and probably earlier, in the Krstic case.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that is right.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: If you could now look at page 3. This is the paragraph -- the first paragraph on the B/C/S version, or page 2, last paragraph of the English version. Here you're talking about the 12th of July. Because in the third paragraph you begin: "On Thursday of the 14th of July at dawn." Let's just be specific about the time that you are talking about. But in the first paragraph you said: "I noticed that the Chetniks were separating the men from their families. That's why I tried to find a better place to hide." So it -- based on this statement, it can be concluded that you saw that yourself?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: No. "Noticed" can also mean to hear. Why not?

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Well, "to notice," first of all --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: I apologise.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: So that we don't go into a discussion about it, "to notice" means to notice personally. "To hear" means to feel with your sense of hearing?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Lazarevic, please move to the next question. I think he has explained. He doesn't agree with you on the meaning of "noticed." He's given you another explanation. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: And I would just point out, if I'm at the same place where I think my friend is, if it could be read in English, which is the official first version, the B/C/S is a translation, it's different, which might help.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Which paragraph -- what paragraph is it?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Unless I'm lost, I thought we were on the top of page 3 in the English.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we have to move another page.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: "As I noticed" in English version. It's last paragraph of page 2.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If it's last paragraph of page 2, then we have to go back one page.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: But he was talking about the top of page 3, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But anyway, let's -- let's close this. He has explained what he understands by that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Continuing with your statement, speaking about the 13th of July, when you testified in the Krstic case, and when you testified about the events of the 13th of July and about how you decided to leave, you said on page 1255 of the Krstic transcript, line 23, 24, you said: "[In English] I simply could not stand it any longer." [Interpretation] These were the words you used at the time. And then to continue on the next page, 1256, lines 4 to 8, you also said: "[In English] I found myself in an even bigger crowd of people because everybody was trying to get out. When I say 'people,' I mean both women and children and a few men were still in the same crowd still. I managed to, after quite a long period of time, that is after an hour or perhaps even more, I somehow managed to make my way to those APCs." [Interpretation] I was quoting the transcript from the Krstic case, which reflects in your best recollection the sense that you had and the general sense of the feeling of the people who happened to be there about the arrival of the buses. Do you agree with what you said, and do you abide by it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: It's very nicely explained, and it's quite precisely explained that I couldn't stand it anymore in that bus that happened to be there, and I decided to leave, and then I found myself in an even closer mass and a denser crowd of people. Everybody wanted to leave. They all wanted to leave at any price, but it was impossible to leave so fast.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. That is just my question about whether this was a precise explanation and whether it was really like that. But can you tell us whether this was at 8.00 in the morning when you set off towards the Dutch APCs? So you needed about an hour to reach them. Can you be a little bit more specific here?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: It's very difficult to talk about timing and to remember precisely the time. I think that it was in the morning. I don't know whether it was 7.00, 7.30, 6.30. Please believe me when I say that I'm not able to remember exactly what time it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But at any -- in any case, it was in the morning, early in the morning?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And if we were to follow that, that you needed about an hour, as you just said, to push through the crowd to reach the Dutch APCs, does that mean that you could have been in the bus at about 9.00 in the morning at the earliest?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: It's the same thing as when we were talking about the starting time. It all depends on that particular time. I said that I couldn't remember exactly what time I set off. We were going to have the finishing time when I said that it was about 7.00 when I thought that we reached Luke. If you're trying to make any calculations and trying to get me to talk about some gap or something, then I think it's the wrong track.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I am just telling you that that is not the case at all. I'm not trying to put anything in your mouth that you do not wish to say, but you could say that at about 10.00 you were at Luke?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Well, I gave you an approximate time. I said that it was very difficult to remember the times and all the details specifically. If you are walking around town and then somebody asks you, "What time were you in such-and-such a shop?" You could give them a time but it would be an estimate. You wouldn't be able to give them the exact time, especially in such difficult circumstances. That makes the whole thing even more difficult.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. I understand that you cannot be sure about the timing, and nobody's asking you to be exact to the minute. But let's say would it be correct to say that you referred Luke in the morning, by noon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes. We could be even more specific. We could say that we got there at about 10.00. It would be half an hour before or half an hour after. So we could be a bit more specific that it was around 10.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: All right. I will not go on asking you anymore about that. Did you also testify in the Krstic case, on page 1256, lines 22 to 25, and you also said that once you passed the Dutch transporter: "[In English] ... and had moved away for the moment and I think that somebody must have called them and they just moved away for a moment and that proved to be a correct assumption later on." [Interpretation] Is this a correct assumption? Did you testify of this in the Krstic case? You can just answer yes or no. I will have to -- I will give you the opportunity to go in detail a little bit further.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, it's true that the Serb soldiers did not go in when we were there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes. The danger of you as a man being separated did exist in front of the bus, but the soldiers were called away, so this made it possible for you to go in.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: I would just like to put a couple more questions to you. When you entered the bus and your trip continued through Bratunac, you passed through Kravica and then you continued on to Luke; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: Yes, that is correct. That is known to everyone.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. When you were in the bus, you described how you, let me say, concealed yourself by hiding between the seats. You had a child that you took and you were sitting like that so you wouldn't be noticed along the way; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: I can describe here to you how the bus has a front and a rear door. I entered through the front door, and I stepped maybe two or three steps inside the bus, and I sat on the floor in a row between two seats, and then women continued to enter after me, and this concentration of women and children around me created a sort of wall around me. So I wasn't visible because I was sitting on the floor; and secondly, I was among the women and children.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Very well. The bus moved along this route all that time; is that correct? The bus continued driving, or were there any stops? Did you make any stops anywhere?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: The bus stopped or was stopped at several places. It was stopped by a group of Serbian soldiers who wanted to see if there were any men in the bus.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: As you were passing through Kravica, you did not stop; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-118
utterances.text: No. The bus did stop in Kravica so that they could look to see if there were any men, since the bus took a while to drive through Kravica because the road was narrow and because there were Serb soldiers aligned along the road, and nearby there were detained men. I assume they were men from Srebrenica. Their hands were tied behind their backs.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: And we will talk about that a little bit later. What I want to ask you is about the point when you reached Tisca?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... because we've only got two minutes left.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Yes, it seems so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So choose whether to put another question, maximum two questions now, or whether we adjourn straight away if you're touching on a new subject.

utterances.speaker: MR. LAZAREVIC
utterances.text: Maybe I should rather ask these questions tomorrow. It's one topic that I need to cover, and maybe it would be better for me to start tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Sir, we didn't manage to finish today. There's still one counsel who wishes to cross-examine you, and that is another 40 minutes or so, but we will continue tomorrow, but within an hour or so you will be out of this courtroom. So in the meantime, now you will be escorted out of this room. You will receive the usual assistance. Go to your hotel and make sure that you do not approach anyone or let anyone approach you to discuss or even to mention the matters on which you are giving evidence today.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you very much, Your Honours, for your patience and the time that you have devoted to this.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can we safely adjourn? Is there anything we -- Mr. Haynes. Go ahead. We have to bring down the curtains. Otherwise if you finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. HAYNES
utterances.text: That could be done while I'm speaking. I just thought that I'd indicate that I've canvassed all my colleagues and -- in relation to the question of protective measures for witnesses in November, and we have no objection to any of the orders sought and we're satisfied that the conditions are met.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much, Mr. Haynes, and the rest of the Defence teams. So we'll prepare the decision and either tomorrow or the day after we'll hand it down. All right. We stand adjourned until tomorrow morning, Thursday, at 9.00. Thank you.
